clue.text: Type of surgery, German, with jabs: they aid mobility

parts.note: in Britain a surgery is a doctor's practice, and a walk-in one takes patients who turn up without an appointment
G is the standard one-letter abbreviation for German
to stick something into a person is to jab them

explanation.walkthrough: Everything before the colon is a scene at a health centre, jabs and all, which is why the German sits there so quietly as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: they aid mobility: the plural matches, and the phrase names the sticks by their job — supports leaned on so that walking stays possible.

clue.text: Diffused a looser spray

indicators.note: Something diffused has been scattered in all directions at once, so the seven letters arrive with their order broken up.

parts.note: seven letters in and seven out, the two Os keeping each other company

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Diffused' as what the answer does rather than as an order given to the two words after it — a can does diffuse things, which is exactly why it sits first.
explanation.definitionFit: spray: the pressurised can of fine mist is called a spray in everyday speech, so the noun swaps straight in.

clue.text: Understood: some work now non-essential

indicators.note: Asking for some of a run of words is asking for a piece of it letter by letter, not for a meaning.

parts.note: five letters run without a break from the end of the first word, through the whole of the second and into the third

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the first word look like a curt reply, and 'non-essential' looks like an instruction to throw something away. Neither is doing any work beyond the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Understood: as past participles they swap directly — a thing that is widely known is widely understood to be so.

clue.text: Barely-there short nightgown covering one — bold bit of licentiousness

indicators.note: a garment covering something goes round it, so the shortened nightgown encloses the next pieces
short means cut off at the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a negligee is a light, flimsy nightgown
I is the Roman numeral for one
B is the typographical abbreviation for bold

indicators.note: a bit of the word here is just its first letter

explanation.surface: A racy description of a skimpy nightie hinting at a little naughtiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims NEGLIGEE to NEGLIGE, and 'covering' puts I, B and L inside it before the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Something negligible is so slight or insignificant that it scarcely exists at all.

clue.text: Drains visible in rest areas in retreat

indicators.note: An army in retreat is going back the way it came, so these four letters are read in the opposite direction.

parts.note: what is on show at a place built for resting: a spa is a resort of baths and treatments

explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' is doing two jobs at once — a health retreat is precisely the sort of place the first half of the clue describes, and the same word is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Drains: to sap someone is to drain their strength little by little, the sense used of energy and morale rather than of water.

clue.text: Floods among the reeds

parts.note: to be among a crowd is to be in it
rushes are the tall stiff marsh plants that grow where reeds do

explanation.walkthrough: Three words make one picture of a riverbank, and there is no indicator anywhere to break the spell. The whole trick is hearing the same phrase as two pieces instead of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Floods: an inrush is a sudden pouring in of water, and the plural matches — both name surges arriving all at once.

clue.text: German child with the French books in here

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer instead of naming it: these are devices, and the clue points at them by what is stored inside them rather than offering a synonym.

parts.note: Kind is the German for child
les is French for 'the' when what follows is plural

explanation.walkthrough: Two languages in six words, and both are asking to be translated rather than pictured — the surface's small child on a French holiday never existed.
explanation.definitionFit: books in here: the answer names Amazon's e-readers, so the definition points at the objects by their contents.

clue.text: Roll up! Not one old nag in bit of horse-racing

indicators.note: A bare 'Not' in front of a piece of wordplay marks that piece as one to take away rather than to add on.

parts.note: to furl a sail or a flag is to roll it up
O is the usual abbreviation for old
a nag is a worn-out horse
the letter that leaves: 'one' here is the article a, taken out of the horse

explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll up!' is a fairground barker's shout, which is what makes the sentence hang together; it is an instruction to a sail instead.
explanation.definitionFit: bit of horse-racing: races are measured in furlongs, an eighth of a mile each, so the vague 'bit' names the unit rather than an event.

clue.text: Dashing, having knocked back some runners?

definitions.meaning: lively and brimming with energy, the way you describe someone who bounds into a room
runner beans, the climbing green pods of every British allotment, are runners — and to knock a plateful back is to get it down you

explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' looks like an instruction to turn something round and 'some' like the start of a hidden word. Both belong to the pub-and-plate picture, and neither is a mechanism here.
explanation.definitionFit: Dashing is 'full of beans' in the sense of brimming energy; the second reading takes the phrase at its word, of someone who has eaten a plate of runner beans.

clue.text: Score and trim root vegetable

parts.note: par is the score a golfer is expected to take at a hole
to snip is to trim with a quick cut of the scissors

explanation.walkthrough: 'Score and trim' reads as two things a cook does to a vegetable, which is precisely what keeps the two separate words from showing.
explanation.definitionFit: root vegetable: definition by example — the parsnip is one particular pale root eaten roasted, not the class of roots itself.

clue.text: Itinerant rashly precipitate

indicators.note: rashly means recklessly, without order, so the letters of precipitate are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A wanderer acts hastily, as though rushing headlong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rashly precipitate' reads as a single instruction to act hastily, and precipitate does mean hasty, but here it is just the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Peripatetic describes someone travelling from place to place, such as a teacher working at several schools, so it means itinerant.

clue.text: Snapping: 'Down with that thing!'

parts.note: a side that is down in a match is behind on the scoreboard
the pronoun that stands in for a thing already pointed at

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks sell it as a protester's shout — a demand that something be got rid of — and a shout is read as one phrase, never as two pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Snapping: to lose it is to lose your self-control, and someone who snaps at people has just done exactly that.

clue.text: Eco option — wanting money, morals abandoned

definitions.note: The definition is a noun phrase while the answer is an adjective; the energy trade uses it as a noun anyway — 'solar is cheaper than gas' — which is the usage the setter is leaning on.

indicators.note: A thing described as wanting is missing something, and what goes missing here is the letter named next to it.
Abandoned behaviour has no restraint on it at all, and letters described that way keep none of their order.

parts.note: the letter that leaves: economists write the money supply as M, and crosswords take M for money
six letters less that M leaves five, and those five are what gets shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a character sketch of someone broke and unscrupulous, so the two instructions look like judgements. Both of them land on the single word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Eco option: solar power is the green choice being pointed at, the sun's energy standing in for the whole phrase.

clue.text: Gosh! Now I will jump around, very loudly — doing this?

definitions.note: The definition is a back-reference rather than a synonym: 'this' is the boast the clue has just made, so the answer has to be read as what that speaker is up to.

indicators.note: Something that jumps around will not stay where it was put, so these letters finish in different places from the ones they started in.

parts.note: eight letters, the exclamation included, handed straight over
ff is the musician's fortissimo, the marking for very loud

explanation.walkthrough: A semi-&lit: the sentence being taken apart for its letters is also the behaviour being defined, so the speaker demonstrates the answer while spelling it.
explanation.definitionFit: doing this?: the definition points back at the speaker of the clue, whose announced leap is exactly the display the answer names.

clue.text: Art gets lubricated

definitions.note: A painter's medium is always spoken of in the plural — 'she works in oils' — so the singular 'Art' fairly defines a plural answer.
definitions.meaning: pigment ground in linseed, and by extension the pictures painted with it
what you do to a hinge or a bicycle chain to stop it squeaking

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the likeliest reading of them is a bloke named Art getting drunk. Nothing in the clue announces that it is two definitions in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Art: oils are the paints and the pictures made with them; the second sense is the verb, since to oil a thing is to get it lubricated.

clue.text: Huge splint, after combustion, cools down?

definitions.note: a verb phrase like the answer; the question mark flags a loose sense, relaxing rather than cooling

indicators.note: after combustion means once burnt up and broken apart, so the letters of huge and splint come out jumbled

explanation.surface: A huge wooden splint that has been burnt then cools off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays against the fire picture: after burning something cools down, and the answer is the relaxed, figurative sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To lighten up is to relax and become less serious, rather like calming or chilling out.

clue.text: Merrily deadheaded herbgrace in town of French literature?

indicators.note: merrily means in a playful, carefree way, so the remaining letters are shuffled
to deadhead a flower is to cut off its head, so the first letter of herbgrace goes

explanation.surface: A gardener happily removes the dead flowers from the herb-of-grace.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb-grace (or herb of grace) is an old name for rue. 'deadheaded' leaves ERBGRACE, which 'Merrily' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Bergerac is a town in south-west France, made famous in literature by the play Cyrano de Bergerac.

clue.text: FBI agent yells, as Spooner tells associates

indicators.note: as Spooner tells signals swapping the opening sounds of the two words, after the Reverend Spooner famous for such slips

parts.note: a Fed is US slang for a federal agent, such as one from the FBI
yells means bellows, a word said 'bell-ohs'; Spooner swaps sounds, and the sounds keep their spelling here

explanation.surface: An FBI man shouting about his colleagues, as reported in Spooner's mangled style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as Spooner tells' swaps the F of FED and the B of BELLOWS, so FED BELLOWS becomes BED FELLOWS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedfellows, as in 'strange bedfellows', are people allied or associated with one another.

clue.text: Almost in pieces, overcome by noise in cinema

indicators.note: Almost a word is not quite all of a word, so the spelling stops one letter short of the end.
To be overcome by something is to be swamped by it, with the other word closing over the top rather than lining up alongside.

parts.note: a din is a continuous racket, and this one opens up to take a passenger
something in pieces is riven, and stopping a letter short of that leaves RIVE

explanation.walkthrough: 'Noise in cinema' reads as a single complaint about other people's popcorn, which is what hides the fact that the last word alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: cinema: the answer is the open-air kind you watch from a parked car, so 'cinema' defines it as one variety of the thing.

clue.text: Treaty very popular in the auditorium

indicators.note: An auditorium is a room built for listening, so what counts is how the words sound in it rather than how they are spelled.

parts.note: a show that is very popular plays to a packed house, and that word said aloud is written quite differently

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the auditorium' looks like more of the picture of a full theatre. It is the instruction, and the picture is what keeps it invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Treaty: a pact is an agreement between parties and a treaty is that agreement between states — the same noun, one narrower than the other.

clue.text: Plays seen here in part of Philadelphia

indicators.note: Asking for part of a name is asking for a run of its letters exactly as they stand, not for a district or a suburb.

parts.note: the city's name carries seven consecutive letters that spell something else, though not from its start

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a neighbourhood in an American city, and American cities do have theatre districts — which is why the geography feels like the answer rather than the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Plays seen here: the Adelphi is a West End theatre on the Strand in London, so 'here' points at a named venue instead of giving a synonym.

clue.text: Getting on with a drink: good

parts.note: the article, taken as the single letter it is
gin is the crossword's default spirit, three letters and always to hand
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.walkthrough: British solvers may want the spelling with an E in the middle; the grid takes the shorter form, and both are current.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting on: 'getting on' is the everyday idiom for growing old, and the answer is that same process as a participle.

clue.text: 15C — shivering, actually

indicators.note: shivering means shaking, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: 15C is read out in words as fifteen C

explanation.surface: Someone shivering at fifteen degrees Celsius, in fact.
explanation.walkthrough: '15C' looks like a cross-reference to 15 across or a temperature, but spelt out as FIFTEEN C it supplies the letters to be shaken.
explanation.definitionFit: In effect means in practice or in reality, so it can stand for actually.

clue.text: Jacques's one with energy rising increasingly, Frank

definitions.note: frank means free and open, so more frank is the comparative, an adjective like the answer

indicators.note: E is energy in physics, and in a down clue rising means that letter moves up one place, above the R

parts.note: the nursery song Frère Jacques calls Jacques a frère, French for brother, so he is one

explanation.surface: Brother Jacques's friend gets more energetic and franker.
explanation.walkthrough: FRERE is French for brother, as in the song Frère Jacques; its final E, standing for energy, rises one place.
explanation.definitionFit: Freer is the comparative of free, and free speech is frank speech, so freer means more outspoken.

clue.text: On vacation — holiday — starts to detest Everyman's hideous alter ego

indicators.note: a place on vacation is emptied, so only the outer letters of holiday stay
the starts of these two words means their first letters

explanation.surface: Someone on holiday finds their dreadful other self, the one everybody loathes.
explanation.walkthrough: In Stevenson's story the respectable Dr Jekyll turns into the brutal Mr Hyde; 'Everyman' here is a general person, not only the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Hyde is the monstrous second personality of Jekyll in Stevenson's novella, the archetypal dark side.

clue.text: Trust son with organ, Times

parts.note: S is the family-tree abbreviation for son
w with a stroke through it is the everyday shorthand for with
the ear is an organ of the body, not of a church or a newspaper
in multiplication you say three by four, so 'times' is the word BY

explanation.walkthrough: The italics dress the last word up as the newspaper, and 'organ' is happy to be one too. Both belong to arithmetic and anatomy instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Trust: to swear by a remedy or a brand is to trust it completely, the verb phrase standing in for the plain verb.

clue.text: Omnipresent, zeitgeisty, expensive medicine putatively inhibiting cuddliness, primarily?

definitions.text: Omnipresent, zeitgeisty, expensive medicine putatively inhibiting cuddliness, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so only the opening character of each word in the run is kept.

parts.words: Omnipresent, zeitgeisty, expensive medicine putatively inhibiting cuddliness
parts.note: seven words, seven initials, taken in the order they are written

explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: the sentence describes the thing and spells it at the same time, and the run of adjectives that would be padding anywhere else is the whole mechanism.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue reads straight: this is the much-discussed and costly weight-loss drug, so 'inhibiting cuddliness' is a description of what it does.

clue.text: Crazy kids reckon fox blown away

indicators.note: crazy means wild or deranged, so the letters of kids reckon fox are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mad children think a fox has been blown off by the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: Knocked for six is a cricket idiom: a six is the maximum score from hitting the ball over the boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: To be knocked for six is to be overwhelmed or astonished, so it means blown away.
